source.title: How to Select Pre-Trained Code Models for Reuse? A Learning Perspective
source.authors: Zhangqian Bi; Yao Wan; Zhao-Yang Chu; Yufei Hu; Junyi Zhang; Hong-Yu Zhang; Guandong Xu; Hai Jin

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream vulnerability-detection accuracy across pre-trained code models of different sizes, a different measure from held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws as motivation for selecting by model size, but does not measure pretraining loss or test power-law fits. Its relevant own results concern downstream accuracy versus model size. Model-selection scores and time costs are not results about the claim versions.
record.test_reason: It compares fine-tuned downstream accuracy across 100 code models (42.5M–3B) to ask whether size predicts downstream performance, a new setting for V6. The models differ in family, data and objective, so size is confounded and the test is weak.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct, with one addition: the authors also conclude that learning-based selection methods (proxy and distribution-based) beat selection by size or data size at far lower cost than brute-force fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: This is a downstream model-selection study, not a reproduction of language-model pretraining-loss scaling measurements. It compares fine-tuned code-model accuracy across model sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors use the same learning rate, epoch count, and batch size across models and select each model's best checkpoint; they note this may not be fair to all models and might favor smaller ones.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Software Analysis, Evolution, and Reengineering
record.problems: The relevant size comparison concerns fine-tuned classification accuracy, not pretraining loss. The paper notes that its shared training configuration may be unfair to some models and might favor smaller ones. Exact values for the full plotted model sweep are not given in the text, and uncertainty for the cited accuracy values is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 plots results for individual PCMs, but the text gives exact accuracy values only for the codet5-small/base example; other plotted values are not transcribed as exact values here. Results for algorithm classification and programming-language identification are not reported as size-versus-performance comparisons.

untested.parts: No shape ablation at fixed size.
No power-law fits in other regimes.
Within-family controlled scaling, relation to pretraining loss, and generation tasks.

missing.what: Ranking quality of 'Model size' as a predictor of fine-tuned accuracy. Devign: NDCG@1/5/10 0.45/0.49/0.54, Rel@1/5/10 0.38/0.44/0.55. POJ-104: Rel@10 1.00. SCC: Rel@10 0.91. Directly quantifies how well size predicts downstream rank.
Model-size ranking across zoos of 10, 30 and 100 models; Rel@1 falls from 0.63 to 0.27 to 0.38 (100 models).
Larger pre-training data does not give higher downstream accuracy for CodeBERT/PLBART variants; confounded by programming language.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is not a scaling-law method aimed at the same question, but a model-selection study in a new setting. Evidence on V6 is weak because model size is confounded with architecture, data, objective and community fine-tuning of variants. The authors note the shared hyperparameters 'might favor smaller ones'. The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation. Rows r2 and r3 duplicate one comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute, including power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude.
Whether small-run power-law fits predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Controlled effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The relation to pretraining loss, and downstream predictability beyond the tested code-model classification setting.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and curvature away from a power law.

rows.subject: 100 PCMs (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained models fine-tuned for vulnerability detection
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream accuracy across PCMs ordered by parameter count.
rows.value: The paper states that a larger PCM does not always yield better performance.
rows.note: Aggregate finding for the tested model collection; the paper does not give one aggregate accuracy value.
rows.check: Qualitative statement only; the paper says larger models do not 'always' do better and gives no overall trend or correlation. Not an absence of any size trend.

rows.subject: Salesforce/codet5-small
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained model fine-tuned for vulnerability detection
rows.operation_detail: Compared its downstream accuracy with the larger Salesforce/codet5-base model.
rows.note: The smaller model has higher accuracy than the stated larger-model comparator.
rows.check: Same comparison as r3, seen from the smaller model. Its state should match r3: the larger model has lower accuracy. Also, the stated sizes (42.5M, 156.57M) are 'specific variants', not the official checkpoints in Table I (60.49M, 222.88M).

rows.subject: Salesforce/codet5-base
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained model fine-tuned for vulnerability detection
rows.operation_detail: Compared its downstream accuracy with the smaller Salesforce/codet5-small model.
rows.note: The larger model has lower accuracy than the stated smaller-model comparator.
rows.check: A single cherry-picked pair of community variants, possibly fine-tuned or trained differently. It is a reversal for this pair only, not a measured trend.

relationships.condition: Heterogeneous zoo of public code models of mixed families, fine-tuned with one shared recipe on classification tasks (mainly Devign)
relationships.reason: The text reports smaller models sometimes beating larger ones (r1, r3) and model-size ranking predicting the best model poorly. Size is confounded with architecture, data and objective, and the authors say the shared recipe may favour small models. Part of this rests on Table II, which no row captures.
relationships.display_finding: Smaller models sometimes outperformed larger ones, with architecture, data, objective, and a shared fine-tuning recipe confounding size rankings.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
